name: Fenoterol

lead: Fenoterol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist used as an inhaled bronchodilator for asthma and, in some countries, to slow preterm labour.
In body-composition circles it is mentioned as a relative of clenbuterol, because beta-2 receptors are involved in fat breakdown and heat production.

paras: It stimulates beta-2 adrenergic receptors, relaxing airway muscle; the same receptor family on fat and brown fat tissue is studied in energy balance.
Common effects are faster heartbeat, tremor and lower potassium. New Zealand studies in the 1980s linked fenoterol inhalers to asthma deaths. It is prescription-only where approved.

chain: Increases fat breakdown and energy output in lab and animal work
angle.text: Some community members group fenoterol with other beta-2 agonists as a possible route to fat loss and a leaner look because these receptors take part in fat mobilisation and heat production. It is a prescription bronchodilator and is not used as a weight-loss drug in medicine.

lead: Fenoterol is a short-acting beta-2 adrenergic agonist developed in the 1970s as a bronchodilator for asthma and other airway disease, and in some countries as a tocolytic to slow preterm labour [1][2]. It relaxes smooth muscle in the airways by stimulating beta-2 receptors, and is marketed in some regions in inhaled forms, including under the Berotec name [3][4].

In looksmaxxing and body-composition discussion, fenoterol appears as one of the beta-2 agonists, a family that includes clenbuterol and salbutamol, which some people associate with fat loss and lean-mass retention. The interest is based on the role of beta-adrenergic receptors in fat breakdown and heat production, which research has explored for decades [5].

Fenoterol is a prescription medicine where it is approved and is not marketed as a weight-loss product. Its main published literature concerns asthma treatment and a well-known series of New Zealand studies in the 1980s that examined an association between fenoterol inhalers and asthma deaths [6][7].
infobox: Inhaled; intravenous and oral in some countries
Asthma, bronchospasm, preterm labour (tocolysis in some countries)
Prescription-only where approved; not available in all countries

paras: Fenoterol is used as a rescue bronchodilator in asthma and in chronic obstructive airway disease, with onset within minutes when inhaled and effects lasting several hours [1][8][9]. A 1979 crossover trial reported that fenoterol's response exceeded terbutaline's at the doses studied [10], and a 1983 trial compared it with salbutamol by nebulisation [11]. It is also combined with ipratropium in some products [4].
In some European countries it has been used intravenously as a tocolytic to delay preterm birth, though it is associated with more maternal side effects than placebo [1].

Online discussion of fenoterol for appearance centres on fat loss and body recomposition, following the pattern of other beta-2 agonists. Participants discuss it as an alternative to clenbuterol in regions where fenoterol inhalers are easier to obtain. It has no approved cosmetic indication.

Fenoterol binds beta-2 adrenoceptors on airway smooth muscle, triggering a signalling cascade that relaxes the muscle and widens the airways [6]. It is more selective for beta-2 than for beta-1 receptors, though at higher doses effects on the heart can occur [6]. Beta-adrenergic receptors on fat and brown adipose tissue are also part of research into thermogenesis and energy balance [5].

Reviews list the predictable effects of short-acting beta agonists as faster heart rate, tremor and changes in serum potassium and glucose, with tolerance developing on continued exposure [12]. The potential for arrhythmia increases with other heart or lung conditions and with low oxygen [12].

Fenoterol is also known for its link with asthma mortality. Case-control studies in New Zealand covering 1981 to 1983 and 1981 to 1987 reported higher odds of death among people prescribed fenoterol metered-dose inhalers, and a Canadian study reported associations between regular beta-agonist use and death or near-death from asthma [13][14][15][16]. Reviews describe fenoterol-related epidemics of increased asthma mortality in the 1970s and 1980s [2][2]. Fenoterol was withdrawn or restricted in some markets afterward [1].
Where it is marketed, fenoterol is a prescription medicine. Availability differs by country, and it is not sold in several markets [1].

The community material about fenoterol is sparse compared with clenbuterol. Mentions describe it as a related beta-2 agonist available in some countries, with discussion focused on fat-loss claims and on cardiovascular side effects such as raised heart rate and tremor.

Human trials of fenoterol are mainly in asthma and COPD. A randomised double-blind crossover trial in 17 asthma patients compared fenoterol and terbutaline with placebo, finding both increased peak expiratory flow [10]. Other trials compared fenoterol with salbutamol by nebulisation and examined initial treatment of acute asthma, including in children [11][17][18]. A randomised trial in 1990 examined regular inhaled beta-agonist treatment in asthma [19].

Registered trials include studies of Berotec inhalers in asthma, COPD and bronchiectasis exercise capacity, a phase 1 study of fenoterol in heart failure, and a post-marketing surveillance study of 2,914 people with chronic obstructive airway disease [3][20][21][22]. A registered early-phase study compared beta-2 adrenergic stimulation with cold exposure for activating human brown fat [23]. A randomised trial also examined fenoterol excretion during recovery from a weight-loss protocol [24]. No trial has been published testing fenoterol as a fat-loss treatment.

Animal work found that chronic beta-2 agonist treatment can change body composition and protein synthesis in rats [25]. Research on brown adipose tissue has examined beta-adrenoceptors as drug targets for obesity [5].
